## About this notebook

A browser notebook over the IPS dated sites graph: Roman findspots dated from samian potters' stamps, published as Linked Open Data. Nothing is installed and nothing is sent anywhere — the graph is fetched as a static file and queried locally with rdflib under Pyodide.

## What this dataset is

Each row is one findspot at one site, dated from the samian potters'
stamps found there. A potter's production period is known from other
evidence; a findspot that yields stamps of several potters can
therefore be dated by combining them.

The interval is deliberately **not** a confidence interval. It is a
"virtual fuzzy year", `m ± k·σ`, where σ decomposes into the inner
fuzziness of each potter's own date range and the scatter of those
ranges' midpoints, and `k` shrinks as the number of stamps grows.
Treating it as a statistical confidence bound would claim far more
than the archaeology supports.

## Two things worth noticing

Dating sharpness (`lado:qInterval`) and depot character
(`lado:qRepetition`) are kept as **separate axes** and never combined
into a single score. Multiplying them would zero out well dated sites
that happen to yield each stamp once.

Negative years are handled in two places at once, on purpose. The
arithmetic runs on a signed number line with its own declared time
reference system (`samian:trs_ips_year`), which is never shifted; the
calendar reading is attached separately as `time:inXSDgYear`. Shifting
only the negative values would tear the scale apart at zero.


## Step 1 — Set up and load the graph

`rdflib` is not pre-bundled with Pyodide, so it is installed with `micropip`.
HTTP has to go through `pyodide.http.pyfetch`: `requests` and `urllib.request`
do not work in the browser.

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| label: setup
#| output: false
import micropip
await micropip.install("rdflib==7.1.1")

from pyodide.http import pyfetch
from rdflib import Graph

GRAPH_URL = "https://leiza-rse.github.io/IPSDatedSites/bundle.ttl"

_cache = {}

async def load(url):
    """Fetch a Turtle file and parse it into a Graph. Cached per URL."""
    if url in _cache:
        return _cache[url]
    resp = await pyfetch(url)
    if resp.status != 200:
        raise RuntimeError(f"{url} -> HTTP {resp.status}")
    g = Graph()
    g.parse(data=await resp.string(), format="turtle")
    _cache[url] = g
    return g

def show(graph, query):
    """Run a query and return the rows as a list of dicts."""
    res = graph.query(PREFIXES + query)
    cols = [str(v) for v in res.vars]
    return [{c: (None if r[i] is None else str(r[i])) for i, c in enumerate(cols)}
            for r in res]

PREFIXES = """
PREFIX samian:  <http://data.archaeology.link/data/samian/>
PREFIX lado:    <http://archaeology.link/ontology#>
PREFIX crm:     <http://www.cidoc-crm.org/cidoc-crm/>
PREFIX crmdig:  <http://www.ics.forth.gr/isl/CRMdig/>
PREFIX time:    <http://www.w3.org/2006/time#>
PREFIX prov:    <http://www.w3.org/ns/prov#>
PREFIX dcat:    <http://www.w3.org/ns/dcat#>
PREFIX dcterms: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/>
PREFIX skos:    <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#>
PREFIX geo:     <http://www.opengis.net/ont/geosparql#>
PREFIX rdfs:    <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
PREFIX xsd:     <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#>"""
```

Now fetch the graph. It is about 0.3 MB and holds the findspot
datings, the full vocabulary, and the rdf:type triples materialised over
`rdfs:subClassOf` — which is why the CIDOC CRM queries below resolve without a
reasoner.

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| label: load-graph
base = await load(GRAPH_URL)
print(f"{len(base)} triples loaded from {GRAPH_URL}")
```

## Step 2 — The figure, as a table

Every row of the box plot, in the order the figure draws them. The interval bounds come out of OWL-Time rather than from a column: the time-span has a beginning and an end, each of which is an instant holding a numeric position on a named scale. That indirection is what lets the calendar reading and the arithmetic position disagree about negative years without either being wrong.

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| label: query-dated-findspots
assert "base" in dir(), "Run the 'load-graph' cell first."
rows = show(base, """
SELECT ?site ?findspot ?from ?to ?span ?qInterval ?nStamps WHERE {
  ?fs a lado:Findspot ; rdfs:label ?findspot ;
      crm:P89_falls_within ?p ; crm:P4_has_time-span ?ts .
  ?p rdfs:label ?site .
  ?ts time:hasBeginning/time:inTimePosition/time:numericPosition ?from ;
      time:hasEnd/time:inTimePosition/time:numericPosition ?to ;
      lado:qInterval ?qInterval ; lado:nStamps ?nStamps ;
      lado:avgDatemin ?order .
  BIND(?to - ?from AS ?span)
}
ORDER BY ?order
""")
print(f"{len(rows)} rows")
for r in rows[:15]:
    print(r)
```

## Step 3 — The same answer in CIDOC CRM alone

No lado: and no time: term appears below, only CIDOC CRM — and it still returns all 41 findspots with their dates. That is the point of the materialised crosswalk: most triplestores perform no RDFS entailment, so the inferred rdf:type triples are written out explicitly rather than left to a reasoner that may never run. Load the vocabulary alone and this query returns nothing.

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| label: query-crm-only
assert "base" in dir(), "Run the 'load-graph' cell first."
rows = show(base, """
SELECT ?place ?findspot ?from ?to WHERE {
  ?fs a crm:E53_Place ; rdfs:label ?findspot ;
      crm:P89_falls_within ?p ; crm:P4_has_time-span ?ts .
  ?p a crm:E53_Place ; rdfs:label ?place .
  ?ts a crm:E52_Time-Span ;
      crm:P82a_begin_of_the_begin ?from ;
      crm:P82b_end_of_the_end ?to .
}
ORDER BY xsd:integer(STR(?from))
""")
print(f"{len(rows)} rows")
for r in rows[:15]:
    print(r)
```

## Step 4 — Where the calendar and the arithmetic part company

The findspots whose interval begins before the year 1. Note that numericPosition and inXSDgYear differ by one: xsd:gYear counts astronomically, so 1 BC is the year 0, whereas the source database counts historically and the arithmetic must stay on an unbroken number line. Rather than silently picking one, the graph carries both and declares its own time reference system for the number line.

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| label: query-era-and-scale
assert "base" in dir(), "Run the 'load-graph' cell first."
rows = show(base, """
SELECT ?site ?findspot ?numeric ?calendar ?scale WHERE {
  ?fs a lado:Findspot ; rdfs:label ?findspot ;
      crm:P89_falls_within ?p ; crm:P4_has_time-span ?ts .
  ?p rdfs:label ?site .
  ?ts time:hasBeginning ?inst .
  ?inst time:inXSDgYear ?calendar ; time:inTimePosition ?pos .
  ?pos time:numericPosition ?numeric ; time:hasTRS ?trs .
  ?trs rdfs:label ?scale .
  FILTER(?numeric < 0)
}
ORDER BY ?numeric
""")
print(f"{len(rows)} rows")
for r in rows[:15]:
    print(r)
```

## Step 5 — Sharply dated, but not a depot

Findspots that are tightly dated (qInterval above 0.55) while showing almost no die repetition (qRepetition below 0.2) — each stamp occurs once or nearly once. These are exactly the sites that a single combined quality score would destroy: multiply the two and Rougham or the Keltengraben at Vindonissa drop to zero, although their dating is among the sharpest in the set. The two axes measure different things and are deliberately never merged.

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| label: query-two-quality-axes
assert "base" in dir(), "Run the 'load-graph' cell first."
rows = show(base, """
SELECT ?site ?findspot ?qInterval ?qRepetition ?nStamps ?nDies ?repetition
WHERE {
  ?fs a lado:Findspot ; rdfs:label ?findspot ;
      crm:P89_falls_within ?p ; crm:P4_has_time-span ?ts .
  ?p rdfs:label ?site .
  ?ts lado:qInterval ?qInterval ; lado:qRepetition ?qRepetition ;
      lado:nStamps ?nStamps ; lado:nDies ?nDies ;
      lado:dieRepetition ?repetition .
  FILTER(?qInterval > 0.55 && ?qRepetition < 0.2)
}
ORDER BY DESC(?qInterval)
""")
print(f"{len(rows)} rows")
for r in rows[:15]:
    print(r)
```

## Step 6 — Sites with more than one findspot

Bregenz contributes four separately dated findspots; Colchester, London, Vindonissa and La Graufesenque two each. This is why the dating hangs on the findspot rather than on the site, and why the URI fragment is a hash of the findspot name taken per site: a site identifier alone could not tell the four Bregenz contexts apart, and they are dated differently.

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| label: query-findspots-per-site
assert "base" in dir(), "Run the 'load-graph' cell first."
rows = show(base, """
SELECT ?site (COUNT(DISTINCT ?fs) AS ?findspots)
       (GROUP_CONCAT(?name; separator=" · ") AS ?names)
WHERE {
  ?fs a lado:Findspot ; rdfs:label ?name ; crm:P89_falls_within ?p .
  ?p rdfs:label ?site .
}
GROUP BY ?site
HAVING (COUNT(DISTINCT ?fs) > 1)
ORDER BY DESC(?findspots) ?site
""")
print(f"{len(rows)} rows")
for r in rows[:15]:
    print(r)
```

## Step 7 — What links out, and what does not

Every site, with its ancient name and its Pleiades identifier where the source has one. The gaps are the interesting part: roughly a third of the sites carry no Pleiades link and most carry no Latin name. Absence here is recorded as absence — no placeholder is invented — so this query doubles as a worklist for the concordance.

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| label: query-external-identifiers
assert "base" in dir(), "Run the 'load-graph' cell first."
rows = show(base, """
SELECT ?site ?ancientName ?pleiades ?findspots WHERE {
  { SELECT ?p (COUNT(DISTINCT ?fs) AS ?findspots) WHERE {
      ?fs a lado:Findspot ; crm:P89_falls_within ?p .
    } GROUP BY ?p }
  ?p rdfs:label ?site .
  OPTIONAL { ?p lado:ancientName ?ancientName }
  OPTIONAL { ?p lado:pleiadesID  ?pleiades }
}
ORDER BY ?site
""")
print(f"{len(rows)} rows")
for r in rows[:15]:
    print(r)
```

## Step 8 — The dates the model was calibrated against

Five events dated by something other than samian — coins, dendrochronology, a volcano, the historical record — and the assemblage each of them bounds. Every one of these intervals must contain its own terminus, because that is the criterion that fixed tau = 6 in the first place, so this query is also a self-test. <code>margin</code> is how much room the model had to spare at the nearer edge: Pompeii is the tightest, which is why it is the reference that binds. Velsen is marked withheld — it appears in the figures but was kept out of the criterion, because activity continued on the site and the terminus may bound the base rather than the assemblage.

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| label: query-termini
assert "base" in dir(), "Run the 'load-graph' cell first."
rows = show(base, """
SELECT ?event ?terminus ?site ?findspot ?from ?to ?margin ?withheld
WHERE {
  ?ev a lado:IndependentTerminus ; rdfs:label ?event ;
      lado:constrains ?fs ;
      crm:P4_has_time-span/time:inTimePosition/time:numericPosition
        ?terminus .
  ?fs rdfs:label ?findspot ; crm:P89_falls_within/rdfs:label ?site ;
      crm:P4_has_time-span ?ts .
  ?ts time:hasBeginning/time:inTimePosition/time:numericPosition ?from ;
      time:hasEnd/time:inTimePosition/time:numericPosition ?to .
  BIND(ROUND(IF(?terminus - ?from < ?to - ?terminus,
                ?terminus - ?from, ?to - ?terminus)) AS ?margin)
  OPTIONAL { ?ev lado:withheldFromCriterion ?withheld }
}
ORDER BY ?margin
""")
print(f"{len(rows)} rows")
for r in rows[:15]:
    print(r)
```

## Step 9 — In use when Vesuvius erupted

The findspots whose modelled interval contains AD 79. Not a claim that anything here was destroyed by the eruption — it is the other way round: an independently dated instant is used as a probe, and these are the assemblages the model puts in circulation at that moment. The map is the point. A horizon scattered across the provinces is what a well-dated ceramic phase looks like; one that clustered would suggest the dating follows excavation history rather than the material.

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| label: query-contemporary-with-vesuvius
assert "base" in dir(), "Run the 'load-graph' cell first."
rows = show(base, """
SELECT ?site ?findspot ?wkt ?from ?to ?colour WHERE {
  ?ev a lado:IndependentTerminus ; rdfs:label ?event ;
      crm:P4_has_time-span ?tsp .
  FILTER(CONTAINS(?event, "Vesuvius"))
  ?ts time:inside ?tsp ;
      time:hasBeginning/time:inTimePosition/time:numericPosition ?from ;
      time:hasEnd/time:inTimePosition/time:numericPosition ?to .
  ?fs crm:P4_has_time-span ?ts ; rdfs:label ?findspot ;
      crm:P89_falls_within ?p .
  ?p rdfs:label ?site ; geo:hasGeometry/geo:asWKT ?wkt .
  ?row lado:renders ?ts ; lado:hexMidpointYear ?colour .
}
ORDER BY ?from
""")
print(f"{len(rows)} rows")
for r in rows[:15]:
    print(r)
```

## Step 10 — Every dating against every fixed point

The whole 41 by 5 grid, counted. Each dating ends before an independent terminus, contains it, or begins after it. Because a terminus is an instant and not an interval, these are OWL-Time's own <code>time:before</code>, <code>time:inside</code> and <code>time:after</code> rather than Allen relations, which hold only between proper intervals. The shape of the table is a sanity check on the corpus: a terminus near the start should have almost nothing before it, one near the end almost nothing after it.

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| label: query-terminus-positions
assert "base" in dir(), "Run the 'load-graph' cell first."
rows = show(base, """
SELECT ?event ?year ?before ?inside ?after WHERE {
  {
    SELECT ?ev
           (SUM(IF(?rel = time:before, 1, 0)) AS ?before)
           (SUM(IF(?rel = time:inside, 1, 0)) AS ?inside)
           (SUM(IF(?rel = time:after, 1, 0)) AS ?after)
    WHERE {
      ?ev a lado:IndependentTerminus ; crm:P4_has_time-span ?tsp .
      ?ts ?rel ?tsp .
      FILTER(?rel IN (time:before, time:inside, time:after))
    }
    GROUP BY ?ev
  }
  ?ev rdfs:label ?event ;
      crm:P4_has_time-span/time:inTimePosition/time:numericPosition
        ?year .
}
ORDER BY ?year
""")
print(f"{len(rows)} rows")
for r in rows[:15]:
    print(r)
```

## Step 11 — How much of the order survives a closer look

The one number the two queries below do not show between them. Every pair of the 41 datings stands in exactly one relation on the modelled interval, so the first row is all 820 pairs. The second counts only those whose relation is unchanged when the intervals are widened to the full span of their potters' date ranges. Just under half. That ratio is the uncertainty of the relative chronology, expressed as a count rather than as a caveat — and it is the reason <code>time:interval*</code> carries the smaller set.

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| label: query-allen-strength
assert "base" in dir(), "Run the 'load-graph' cell first."
rows = show(base, """
SELECT ?reading (COUNT(*) AS ?assertions) (COUNT(*)/2 AS ?pairs)
WHERE {
  { ?a ?p ?b .
    ?a a lado:FindspotDating . ?b a lado:FindspotDating .
    FILTER(STRSTARTS(STR(?p), CONCAT(STR(lado:), "possibly")))
    BIND("holds on the modelled interval (lado:possibly*)" AS ?reading) }
  UNION
  { ?a ?p ?b .
    ?a a lado:FindspotDating . ?b a lado:FindspotDating .
    FILTER(STRSTARTS(STR(?p), CONCAT(STR(time:), "interval")))
    BIND("survives both readings (time:interval*)" AS ?reading) }
}
GROUP BY ?reading
ORDER BY DESC(?assertions)
""")
print(f"{len(rows)} rows")
for r in rows[:15]:
    print(r)
```

## Step 12 — What came before what — the complete matrix

Every pair of datings stands in exactly one of Allen's thirteen relations, computed on the modelled interval [eff_start, eff_end] and published under <code>lado:possibly*</code>. Complete means countable: the numbers below add up to all 820 pairs of 41 findspots, so a missing relation is a missing pair rather than a silence that could mean anything. Note how lopsided the result is — two thirds of all pairs are simple precedence, which is what a corpus spread over three centuries looks like.

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| label: query-allen-possible
assert "base" in dir(), "Run the 'load-graph' cell first."
rows = show(base, """
SELECT ?relation (COUNT(*) AS ?assertions) WHERE {
  ?a ?p ?b .
  ?a a lado:FindspotDating .
  ?b a lado:FindspotDating .
  FILTER(STRSTARTS(STR(?p), CONCAT(STR(lado:), "possibly")))
  BIND(REPLACE(STR(?p), "^.*#possibly", "") AS ?relation)
}
GROUP BY ?relation
ORDER BY DESC(?assertions)
""")
print(f"{len(rows)} rows")
for r in rows[:15]:
    print(r)
```

## Step 13 — The same question in OWL-Time alone

No <code>lado:</code> predicate appears below — only OWL-Time's own interval relations. It works, and it deliberately returns FEWER pairs than the query above. OWL-Time relations are sharp: there is no way to say "before, probably". So only the relations that survive a more generous reading of the bounds are asserted with them, and the rest live under <code>lado:possibly*</code> where the hedge is visible. This is not OWL-Time falling short. It is a vocabulary without a notion of uncertainty saying exactly as much as it can support — and the gap between the two counts is the uncertainty, made countable.

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| label: query-allen-time-only
assert "base" in dir(), "Run the 'load-graph' cell first."
rows = show(base, """
SELECT ?relation (COUNT(*) AS ?assertions) WHERE {
  ?a ?p ?b .
  ?a time:hasBeginning ?ab .
  ?b time:hasBeginning ?bb .
  FILTER(STRSTARTS(STR(?p), CONCAT(STR(time:), "interval")))
  BIND(REPLACE(STR(?p), "^.*#interval", "") AS ?relation)
}
GROUP BY ?relation
ORDER BY DESC(?assertions)
""")
print(f"{len(rows)} rows")
for r in rows[:15]:
    print(r)
```

## Step 14 — Why an order stops holding

The pairs that are ordered on the modelled intervals but not once the evidence is read generously. The columns are the bounds the relation is actually computed from, and the gap between them — sorted with the narrowest first, because those are the claims that fail soonest. Read the last two columns beside it: the modelled intervals are a year apart while the potters' date ranges overlap by decades. That is the whole distinction in one line, and it is why these pairs carry <code>lado:possiblyBefore</code> and not <code>time:intervalBefore</code>.

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| label: query-allen-unstable
assert "base" in dir(), "Run the 'load-graph' cell first."
rows = show(base, """
SELECT ?earlier ?ends ?later ?begins ?gap ?evidenceEndsA ?evidenceBeginsB
WHERE {
  ?tsA lado:possiblyBefore ?tsB .
  FILTER NOT EXISTS { ?tsA time:intervalBefore ?tsB }
  ?fsA crm:P4_has_time-span ?tsA ; rdfs:label ?earlier .
  ?fsB crm:P4_has_time-span ?tsB ; rdfs:label ?later .
  ?tsA time:hasEnd/time:inTimePosition/time:numericPosition ?ends ;
       lado:maxDatemax ?evidenceEndsA .
  ?tsB time:hasBeginning/time:inTimePosition/time:numericPosition ?begins ;
       lado:minDatemin ?evidenceBeginsB .
  BIND(ROUND(?begins - ?ends) AS ?gap)
}
ORDER BY ?gap
LIMIT 25
""")
print(f"{len(rows)} rows")
for r in rows[:15]:
    print(r)
```

## Step 15 — Everything a map needs, in one query

Coordinates, interval and colour for each findspot. The point sits on the discovery site rather than the findspot, because that is where the source records it — the four Bregenz contexts share one coordinate, and a map that wants them apart has to spread them itself rather than pretend the data distinguishes them. The colour is presentation and is published as such, on the plot row alongside the other "visual only" quantities, never on the time-span.

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| label: query-map-layer
assert "base" in dir(), "Run the 'load-graph' cell first."
rows = show(base, """
SELECT ?site ?findspot ?wkt ?from ?to ?norm ?colour WHERE {
  ?fs a lado:Findspot ; rdfs:label ?findspot ;
      crm:P89_falls_within ?p ; crm:P4_has_time-span ?ts .
  ?p rdfs:label ?site ; geo:hasGeometry/geo:asWKT ?wkt .
  ?ts time:hasBeginning/time:inTimePosition/time:numericPosition ?from ;
      time:hasEnd/time:inTimePosition/time:numericPosition ?to .
  ?row lado:renders ?ts ;
       lado:normQInterval ?norm ; lado:hexQInterval ?colour .
}
ORDER BY ?from
""")
print(f"{len(rows)} rows")
for r in rows[:15]:
    print(r)
```

## Step 16 — How the colours were made

A colour in a dataset is usually an assertion nobody can check. These can be: each axis publishes its ramp stops, its interpolation and the domain the values were stretched onto, so any hex value in the graph can be recomputed from the graph alone. Watch <code>lado:domainBasis</code> — an observed domain is read off this corpus, which means adding a findspot can change the colour of one that did not change at all. The chronological axis avoids red-green on purpose: late material is not worse material.

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| label: query-colour-axes
assert "base" in dir(), "Run the 'load-graph' cell first."
rows = show(base, """
SELECT ?axis ?source ?ramp ?scale ?basis ?min ?max ?stops WHERE {
  ?a a lado:ColourAxis ; lado:colourSource ?src ;
     lado:rampName ?ramp ; lado:rampStops ?stops ;
     lado:domainScale ?scale ; lado:domainBasis ?basis ;
     lado:domainMin ?min ; lado:domainMax ?max .
  BIND(REPLACE(STR(?a), "^.*/", "") AS ?axis)
  BIND(REPLACE(STR(?src), "^.*#", "") AS ?source)
}
ORDER BY ?axis
""")
print(f"{len(rows)} rows")
for r in rows[:15]:
    print(r)
```

## Step 17 — Which method produced these dates

The parameters are in the graph, not only in the paper. Each dating is generated by an activity, and that activity records the plan it followed — so a consumer can ask what k, τ, t₀ and the era convention were, and which datemax values the source query excluded, without reading any prose. τ and lado:referenceLength are unrelated quantities that happened to carry the same value until τ was calibrated: τ governs how fast the interval tightens as stamps accumulate, t₀ is the fixed length against which qStart and qEnd are read. lado:calibrationBasis says how τ was obtained, and lado:calibratedAgainst names the findspots it was fitted to — try following those IRIs. The excluded datemax values are an inherited filter whose justification is still open; publishing them is how that stays visible.

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| label: query-provenance
assert "base" in dir(), "Run the 'load-graph' cell first."
rows = show(base, """
SELECT ?software ?model ?kMin ?kMax ?tau ?t0 ?w ?era
       (GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT STR(?ex); separator=", ") AS ?excludedDatemax)
       (COUNT(DISTINCT ?ts) AS ?datings)
WHERE {
  ?ts a lado:FindspotDating ; prov:wasGeneratedBy ?act .
  ?act crm:P33_used_specific_technique ?m ;
       crm:P14_carried_out_by ?agent .
  ?agent rdfs:label ?software .
  ?m rdfs:label ?model ; lado:kMin ?kMin ; lado:kMax ?kMax ;
     lado:tau ?tau ; lado:referenceLength ?t0 ;
     lado:volumeWeight ?w ; lado:eraConvention ?era ;
     lado:excludedDatemax ?ex .
}
GROUP BY ?software ?model ?kMin ?kMax ?tau ?t0 ?w ?era
""")
print(f"{len(rows)} rows")
for r in rows[:15]:
    print(r)
```

## Where this comes from

Every query above is generated from `queries.yaml` in the
[IPSDatedSites repository](https://github.com/leiza-rse/IPSDatedSites), which
also produces the [browser query page](https://leiza-rse.github.io/IPSDatedSites/query/)
and the plain `.rq` files. One source, three products, so they cannot drift
apart — and each query is executed against the real graph at build time, with
an empty result failing the build.
